newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: FEATURE - Balkans in struggle to supply enough bread.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Balkans in struggle to supply enough bread.

text.p: Political upheaval, economic turmoil and the aftermath of war in former Yugoslavia has left southeastern Europe, once rich in grain, struggling to meet its requirements for staple bread.
Serbia, long considered the bread basket of the Balkans, faces a protracted struggle to get its harvests back up to historic levels.
Albania said on Tuesday it faced a serious food crisis because of looting of government reserves and the collapse of the trading system during the current unrest.
Officials hope that the special highly-paid government police can prevent further looting of grain reserves, estimated at 80,000 tonnes.

Bulgarians have been queuing for bread. The prosecutor general is investigating whether charges of negligence would be justified against the ex-farm minister for exporting more than 827,280 tonnes of grain for 7.141 billion levs ($4.5 million) from the 1994-1995 harvest.
Romania, once an exporter, may have to import to cover grain shortages in the first half of this year.
Croatia is likely to have to import wheat this year, despite an increase in output, and farmers in Hungary cannot afford fertiliser.
Western experts see imports slowing and harvests getting bigger. But exact figures are hard to pinpoint, they said in response to a Reuters survey of the region's grain crisis.
"Unfortunately agricultural production here is in the hands of God and the entire production relies on weather conditions," one Balkan government official said.
YUGOSLAV SHORTAGE EXACERBATED BY EXPORTS

Serbia and Montenegro, present-day Yugoslavia, will take at least seven years to raise output to pre-1991 levels, according to a senior government official. The country faces a shortage after its worst harvest in 25 years and excessive exports last year.
Industry sources say Yugoslavia recently bought up to 100,000 tonnes from Argentina, France, Germany, Austria and Hungary.
Yugoslavia needs around 500,000 tonnes of wheat before the new harvest to secure an estimated 2.5 million tonnes needed to feed its 10 million people and around 500,000 refugees, analysts say.

But in 1995, farmers planted scarcely more than half the area sown the previous year and fuel shortages for tractors helped push the 1996 harvest to a record low of 1.5 million tonnes, down from 2.97 million tonnes. Crop yields were the lowest since 1972.

Empty grain stores forced the government to increase wheat area planted in 1996 to about 850,000 hectares, the average over the past 10 years, and Yugoslavia expects to harvest two to 2.5 million tonnes of wheat this year.
Officials estimate that this means there will be around one million tonnes of wheat and as much maize for export by end-1997.
NO INCENTIVE TO PLANT WHEAT IN BULGARIA
In Bulgaria, bread queues and empty shelves have been a daily sight in recent weeks as the country struggles with a grain shortage rooted in uncontrolled exports two years ago.
Subsequently Bulgaria had to import 198,933 tonnes of grain at a cost of 6.456 billion levs.
An interim cabinet which took office on February 13 immediately released grain from reserves.

It also sold forward about 269,000 tonnes of new crop in exchange for immediate imports and machinery, which Agriculture Minister Roumen Hristov says was as much as it could afford without creating future shortages.

Farmers are being pinched between rising costs and low controlled internal prices, although last-minute incentives by the former socialist government meant that autumn sowing was close to a 1.6 million hectare target.
Hristov said the local wheat price at $85 to $100 per tonne was well below world levels but controls could not be lifted without measures to protect the poor, which Bulgaria could not afford.
Input prices have been freed but inflation and a falling currency has hit farmers. For spring sowing, Hristov said fertiliser manufacturers had offered 10 percent discounts.
"We will secure the winter crop and spring sowing to ensure the incoming government does not suffer a grain crisis," Hristov said. Elections are due on April 19.
The International Grains Council has estimated Bulgarian wheat imports for 1996/97 at a high 600,000 tonnes although one trade source said it might be closer to 500,000 tonnes.
Bulgaria will use World Bank credit to buy some 170,000 tonnes and Poland has agreed to supply 100,000 tonnes of wheat against exports of the same amount from the new crop.

Bulgaria has granted tenders to international grain trader Glencore and Bulgaria's Nada to supply 100,000 tonnes against forward contracts to export 134,000 tonnes from the new crop. Another 35,000 tonnes from the new crop has been exchanged for combine harvesters.

Hristov, who said Bulgaria now needed only about 70,000 tonnes to cover the gap until the next harvest, has visited Germany but won only a promise of support for efforts to win European Union (EU) aid.
Germany has asked EU farm ministers to discuss Bulgaria's request for 100,000 tonnes of soft wheat as food aid.
ROMANIA FALLS BACK ON STRATEGIC RESERVES

In Romania, the farm ministry said a shortage of wheat may force it to import to cover demand for bread in the first half of 1997. The farm ministry has used some 550,000 tonnes from strategic reserves to supply bakeries.
Once an exporter, Romania suffered crop damage after a long winter. In 1996 the harvest was less than 60 percent of a 1995 bumper crop of some 7.8 million tonnes of which 1.3 million were exported.

The ministry has not issued a 1997 forecast for grain crops but data earlier this year showed Romania sowed more than 2.3 million hectares of wheat and rye last autumn. It is expecting a wheat crop this year of around 6.0 million tonnes.
Agriculture minister Dinu Gavrilescu said last week that Romania planned to set up a hard currency fund of around $60 million for wheat imports to complete the country's reserves if necessary.
CROATIA MAY BE FORCED TO IMPORT
Croatia will probably have to import wheat this year, despite an expected increase in production.

After a harrowing experience in 1996, when it exported wheat in expectation of a good harvest only to be disappointed, stocks turned out to be less than expected and autumn sowings were increased by almost 30 percent.
HUNGARY'S FARMERS CANNOT AFFORD FERTILISER
A major problem in Hungary is that farmers cannot afford enough spring fertiliser. Fertiliser usage has fallen sharply since the end of communism.
Farm ministry figures say the fertilised area shrank to 1.85 million hectares in 1995 from 4.4 million in 1985. In the same period fertiliser usage per hectare dropped to 40 kg from 220 kg.
Benedek Fulop, state secretary of the agriculture ministry said he hoped that this year fertiliser usage per hectare would increase.
Crop estimates for Hungary are not available, but the area under wheat is around 1.13 million hectares, up from last year's 1.06 million, with that sown with maize unchanged.
-- Compiled from reports by Reuters correspondents in Belgrade, Bucharest, Budapest, London, Paris, Sofia and Zagreb. ($ = 1575 Bulgarian Levs)
